docs.text: Nicrypt-Stego API Spec (v1) ¶ Decision: REST + JSON Rationale: easiest enterprise integration, works with standard gateways, audit tooling, and log pipelines. gRPC can be added later as a parallel interface. Base URL - /v1 Auth - Bearer tokens (JWT or opaque) via Authorization header. - Optional mTLS for internal deployments. - All write operations require scope-based authorization. - Multi-tenant support via org_id in JWT (or X-Org-Id header). - Rate limits and quotas are enforced per org. Content Types - Request: application/json - Response: application/json Common Fields - model_name: string - bits_per_token: integer (1-4, default 2) - max_new_tokens: integer (default 200) - model_hash: string (server-computed, stable hash of model + tokenizer + config + sampling params) - request_id: string (server-generated UUID) - org_id: string (derived from JWT or X-Org-Id header) Endpoints 1) Create key profile POST /v1/keys Request { "name": "legal-team-2026", "rotation_policy": "annual", "metadata": { "owner": "legal", "purpose": "authorship-provenance" } } Response { "key_id": "key_9f4d2", "name": "legal-team-2026", "rotation_policy": "annual", "created_at": "2026-02-13T10:30:00Z" } 2) List key profiles GET /v1/keys Response { "keys": [ { "key_id": "key_9f4d2", "name": "legal-team-2026", "rotation_policy": "annual", "created_at": "2026-02-13T10:30:00Z" } ] } Note: Keys are scoped to org_id. Requests from one org cannot list or rotate keys from another org. 3) Rotate key POST /v1/keys/{key_id}/rotate Response { "key_id": "key_9f4d2", "rotated_at": "2026-02-13T10:40:00Z", "status": "rotated" } 4) Embed provenance (encrypt + embed) POST /v1/provenance/embed Request { "secret": "Alice Johnson, 2026-02-12, CC-BY-NC", "cover_prompt": "a short compliance memo about data retention", "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B", "bits_per_token": 2, "max_new_tokens": 220, "key_id": "key_9f4d2" } Response { "request_id": "req_1b2c3", "stego_text": "...", "model_hash": "mhash_7e83...", "payload_bytes": 92, "tokens_used": 214 } 5) Embed ciphertext (embed only) POST /v1/provenance/embed_cipher Request { "ciphertext": "gAAAAABl...", "cover_prompt": "a short compliance memo about data retention", "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B", "bits_per_token": 2, "max_new_tokens": 220 } Response { "request_id": "req_1b2c3", "stego_text": "...", "model_hash": "mhash_7e83...", "payload_bytes": 132, "tokens_used": 214 } 6) Extract ciphertext POST /v1/provenance/extract Request { "stego_text": "...", "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B", "bits_per_token": 2 } Response { "request_id": "req_4d5e6", "ciphertext": "gAAAAABl...", "model_hash": "mhash_7e83...", "confidence": 0.93 } 7) Verify (extract + decrypt) POST /v1/provenance/verify Request { "stego_text": "...", "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B", "bits_per_token": 2, "key_id": "key_9f4d2" } Response { "request_id": "req_4d5e6", "secret": "Alice Johnson, 2026-02-12, CC-BY-NC", "verified": true, "model_hash": "mhash_7e83...", "metadata": { "detected": true, "tampered": false } } 8) List models GET /v1/models Response { "models": [ { "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B", "model_hash": "mhash_7e83...", "context_length": 8192, "notes": "Production baseline" } ] } Note: Model pull/status tracking is scoped per org. 9) Pull model POST /v1/models/pull Request { "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B" } Response { "status": "queued", "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B" } Note: Model pull status is stored per org_id. 10) Health GET /v1/health Response { "status": "ok", "uptime_s": 104233 } 11) Metrics GET /v1/metrics Response { "format": "prometheus" } Note: Metrics requires auth and is scoped by org_id for rate limiting. Error Model All errors return: { "request_id": "req_...", "error": { "code": "MODEL_NOT_FOUND", "message": "Model not available on server", "details": { "model_name": "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B" } } } Error Codes - INVALID_REQUEST - AUTH_REQUIRED - AUTH_FORBIDDEN - KEY_NOT_FOUND - KEY_ROTATION_FAILED - MODEL_NOT_FOUND - MODEL_MISMATCH - INVALID_BITS_PER_TOKEN - PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE - EXTRACTION_FAILED - DECRYPTION_FAILED - RATE_LIMITED - INTERNAL_ERROR Security Constraints - Scope-based access control (example scopes: provenance:embed, provenance:verify, keys:manage, models:read, models:pull). - All provenance write operations logged with request_id, key_id, model_hash, and payload_bytes. - Optional tamper-evidence: append audit hash to server logs (hash chain per day). - mTLS optional for internal deployments. - Encrypt key material at rest using KMS or HSM. Notes - Deterministic settings required for extraction. The server pins model_name, tokenizer version, and sampling parameters into model_hash. - If model_hash mismatch is detected, extraction returns MODEL_MISMATCH unless override is allowed.

docs.text: Audit Logging & Retention ¶ Overview - Audit logging is append-only JSONL for compliance and provenance tracking. - Enable via environment variables and keep logs on a secured volume. Environment variables - AUDIT_LOG_ENABLED=1 - AUDIT_LOG_PATH=/var/log/nicrypt/audit.jsonl - AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS=30 - AUDIT_LOG_PARTITION=1 Sample audit record {"ts":"2026-02-15T22:11:22.000000+00:00","request_id":"req_abc123","org_id":"org_a","method":"POST","path":"/v1/provenance/embed","status":200,"client_ip":"127.0.0.1","user_agent":"curl/8.5.0"} Export (since timestamp) python scripts/export_audit.py --path /var/log/nicrypt/audit.jsonl --since 2026-02-15T00:00:00+00:00 Export (partitioned logs) python scripts/export_audit.py --path /var/log/nicrypt --org-id org_a --since 2026-02-15T00:00:00+00:00 Prune (retention) python scripts/prune_audit.py --path /var/log/nicrypt/audit.jsonl --days 30 Prune (partitioned logs) python scripts/prune_audit.py --path /var/log/nicrypt --days 30 Partitioned logs - When AUDIT_LOG_PARTITION=1, logs are written per org_id. - If AUDIT_LOG_PATH is a directory, files are named audit_<org_id>.jsonl . - If AUDIT_LOG_PATH is a file, the org_id is appended to the filename.

docs.text: Azure Deployment (Institutional Grade) ¶ Overview This guide outlines a reference architecture for running Nicrypt‑Stego in Azure. Recommended Components - Azure Container Apps or App Service (API) - Azure Key Vault (JWT secrets, nicrypt keys) - Azure Storage or Log Analytics (audit logs) - Azure Email Communication Services or Exchange Online (mail) Reference Flow 1) Outbound mail passes through a relay (or Logic App) that injects X‑Provenance headers. 2) Inbound mail is verified by a header verification function. 3) Verification result is stamped as X‑Provenance‑Verified. Deployment Steps (High Level) 1) Containerize the API. 2) Deploy to Azure Container Apps. 3) Store JWT secrets and ENC keys in Key Vault. 4) Configure outbound relay to call /crypto/encrypt for header creation. 5) Configure inbound verification to call /provenance/verify_headers. Minimal Environment Variables API_BASE=https://<your-app>.azurecontainerapps.io/v1 JWT_SECRET=<stored in Key Vault> ENC_PASSWORD=<stored in Key Vault> ENC_SALT=<stored in Key Vault> Notes - Use managed identity for Key Vault access. - Enforce HTTPS only. - Add rate limiting and IP allowlists for institutional networks. Scripts and Diagram - poc/azure_deploy.sh for Azure CLI deployment. - docs/AZURE_ARCHITECTURE.mmd for reference architecture. - docs/AZURE_ARCHITECTURE.png rendered diagram. Diagram (Rendered)

docs.text: Certificate Provenance Sprint (Institutions) ¶ Objective Enable institutions (universities, regulators, standards bureaus) to issue electronic certificates that recipients can verify as authentic and untampered. Why it matters - Prevent forged qualification certificates and compliance letters. - Allow third‑party verification without contacting the issuer. - Preserve integrity even if the PDF is forwarded outside the original email. Scope Two verification surfaces: 1) Email transport (headers + attachment provenance). 2) Document itself (embedded metadata / portal verification). Deliverables 1) Issuance workflow (PDF) - [x] Script to embed provenance metadata into PDF/DOCX at issuance time ( scripts/issue_certificate.py ). - [x] Attach certificate ID + issuer ID + recipient ID + org ID + timestamp fields (embedded metadata). - [x] Record issuance manifest (JSONL) for audit ( CERT_ISSUANCE_MANIFEST_PATH ). 2) Email delivery flow - [x] Gateway stamps attachment provenance for certificate PDFs (reuse embedded metadata). - Set PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENT_MODE=metadata on poc/smtp_relay.py so X-Provenance-Attachment uses the attachment's embedded X-Provenance-Ciphertext (instead of generating a hash-only claim). - [ ] Optional NS-SIGNATURE line in email body (visible trust line). - [ ] Thunderbird/Gmail/Outlook verification surfaces show attachment status. 3) Standalone verification - [ ] CLI to verify a certificate PDF offline (no email). - [x] API endpoint to verify PDF/DOCX provenance ( POST /v1/certificates/verify ). - [x] CLI helper to call API verify ( scripts/verify_certificate.py ). - [ ] “Verify on portal” simple web flow (paste/upload). 4) Tamper detection - [x] Hash mismatch returns explicit status (tampered). - [x] Partial validation logic (valid issuer vs missing provenance vs tampered; reason surfaced in response). 5) Documentation - [ ] Issuer guide (what to embed, issuance steps). - [ ] Recipient guide (how to verify via email or file upload). - [ ] Threat model (forgery, re‑use, partial tamper). Exit Criteria - At least one end‑to‑end demo: - Issue PDF -> send via gateway -> verify in mail client. - Verify the same PDF offline using CLI/API. - Docs published and linked from Docs Index. Suggested APIs - POST /v1/certificates/issue (metadata + file -> provenance‑embedded file) - POST /v1/certificates/verify (file -> verified + issuer + cert_id) Notes - This uses existing gateway attachment provenance + metadata embedding work. - Certificates should remain visually unchanged; provenance is stored in metadata.

Exit Criteria - At least one end‑to‑end demo: - Issue PDF -> send via gateway -> verify in mail client. - Verify the same PDF offline using CLI/API. - Docs published and linked from Docs Index. docs.text: Document Workflow (Readable by Default) ¶ Goal - Keep documents (research papers, reports, legal docs) fully readable. - Attach provenance without changing visible content. Recommended Approach 1) Extract text from the document. 2) Create a provenance ciphertext from the secret. 3) Store the ciphertext in metadata (not in the visible body). Why this works - The original document remains unchanged and readable. - Metadata travels with the file in most enterprise workflows. - Verification can happen at gateways or client tools without altering content. PDF (recommended) - Store metadata in XMP or custom PDF metadata fields. - Use keys like: - X-Provenance-Ciphertext - X-Provenance-Model - X-Provenance-Bpt - X-Provenance-Timestamp DOCX (recommended) - Use custom document properties: - X-Provenance-Ciphertext - X-Provenance-Model - X-Provenance-Bpt - X-Provenance-Timestamp Verification flow 1) Extract metadata. 2) Call /v1/provenance/verify_headers with those fields mapped into headers. 3) If verified, display a badge or audit stamp. Notes - Some platforms strip metadata. For those, use gateway stamping or archive systems. - For high-risk flows, keep a secondary copy of the ciphertext in a secure audit log. Certificate issuance For institution-issued certificates and reprints, see docs/CERTIFICATE_PROVENANCE_SPRINT.md . Email Provenance: Verified Sender for Anti‑Scam Email ¶ Purpose Provide cryptographic proof that an email was authored by a legitimate organization, enabling recipients and mail systems to detect impersonation and phishing. Related - Certificate issuance and verification: docs/CERTIFICATE_PROVENANCE_SPRINT.md Email vs Certificate Provenance (Quick Comparison) See docs/EMAIL_VS_CERTIFICATE_COMPARISON.md . Goals - Stop sender impersonation even when SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass or are bypassed. - Verify the content itself, not just the sending domain. - Make verification visible to users via a simple trust indicator. - Support on‑prem deployments for regulated institutions. Non‑Goals - Replace SPF/DKIM/DMARC. This complements them. - Guarantee safety of all links or attachments. - Prevent all social engineering. It verifies origin only. High‑Level Flow Outbound (Sender Organization) 1. Compose email content. 2. Generate provenance payload (org, timestamp, campaign, signer id). 3. Encrypt payload with Nicrypt (institution‑managed keys). 4. Embed ciphertext into the email body using steganography. 5. Send email normally. Inbound (Recipient) 1. Mail gateway or client extracts ciphertext from body. 2. Decrypts using the institution’s public verification path (or shared key). 3. Verifies model hash and key id. 4. Shows Verified/Unverified status in the UI. Architecture Options Mail Gateway Integration (Recommended) Outbound: inject provenance in the final hop before SMTP. Inbound: verify for internal recipients and annotate headers. Pros: centralized, scalable, no client plugins required. Cons: requires gateway integration and routing changes. Client Plugin (Outlook / Gmail) Outbound: plugin embeds on send. Inbound: plugin verifies and renders badge. Pros: no gateway changes, faster pilot. Cons: per‑user installation and updates. Application‑Level Integration For custom CRM or internal portals that send email. Embed and verify within the app’s email pipeline. Verification UX - Verified: “Verified Sender” badge with org name and timestamp. - Unverified: “Sender not verified” warning with a short explanation. - Tampered: “Content altered” warning if extraction fails or mismatches. Provenance Payload Format (Example) org=AcmeBank|dept=Consumer|timestamp=2026-02-15T10:32Z|campaign=FraudAlert|key_id=key_9f4d2 Security Model - Keys remain inside the institution’s boundary. - Only authorized systems can encrypt (embed). - Verification can be performed by recipients or gateways using allowed keys. - Model hash ties the message to the configured embedding model for consistency. Threats Addressed - Domain spoofing and look‑alike domains. - Compromised forwarding chains. - Content forgery and copy‑paste attacks. Threats Not Fully Addressed - A compromised sender system (attacker can embed valid provenance). - Social engineering that uses genuine verified messages. - Malicious links or attachments (requires separate scanning). Operational Considerations - Key rotation: rotate keys on a schedule and maintain a grace window for verification. - Model locking: fix model hash for long‑term verification. - Policy: define which communications must be verified (e.g., finance, HR, compliance). - Logs: record verification outcomes for audit and incident response. Integration Steps Phase 1: Pilot - Pick one high‑risk communication stream (bank alerts or HR memos). - Deploy embedding at send time only. - Measure verification success and false negatives. Phase 2: Verification UI - Add badge to internal mail client or gateway‑injected header. - Add warnings for unverified messages. Phase 3: Institution‑wide - Extend to all official communications. - Enforce verified status for trusted channels. API Usage (Minimal) Embed (Outbound) POST /v1/provenance/embed Body: { "secret": "org=AcmeBank|dept=Consumer|timestamp=2026-02-15T10:32Z|campaign=FraudAlert", "cover_prompt": "Subject: Policy Update...", "backend": "mvp", "bits_per_token": 3, "max_new_tokens": 700 } Verify (Inbound) POST /v1/provenance/verify Body: { "ciphertext": "gAAAAABl...5g", "model_name": "sshleifer/tiny-gpt2", "bits_per_token": 4 } Stego Quality Examples (Embed Cipher) These examples use POST /v1/provenance/embed_cipher so you can demonstrate "innocent" cover text while embedding an existing ciphertext. Config notes: - Demo model: sshleifer/tiny-gpt2 (local + lightweight). - ECC: ecc_mode="reed-solomon" with ecc_symbols=16 for robustness. - stego_text below is representative output style (your exact text will vary). Hello,
We’re reaching out to confirm a recent security update to how we communicate with you.

Scripted issuance (CLI) TOKEN="..." SENDER="Nordea Bank Oy" NOTE="Best regards" scripts/signature_token.sh PowerShell $env:TOKEN="..." $env:SENDER="Nordea Bank Oy" $env:NOTE="Best regards" .\scripts\signature_token.ps1 Gateway automation (no user action) - Set SIGNATURE_MODE=visible in the SMTP relay. - The relay appends NS-SIGNATURE: ... to outgoing emails automatically. - Optional: set PROVENANCE_SENDER and PROVENANCE_SIGNATURE_NOTE for consistent branding. Diagram (Outlook → Relay → Internet) flowchart LR A["Outlook Client"] --> B["SMTP Relay (Nicrypt Gateway)"] B --> C["Internet / Recipient MX"] B --> D["Signature Token API"] D --> B B --> E["Adds NS-SIGNATURE to Body + Headers"] Practical use cases - Customer service and banking alerts: append a verifiable signature line. - HR and compliance emails: prove the sender without altering the body. - Press releases and public announcements: readers can verify authenticity. - Support tickets and incident responses: add a tamper-evident signature line. Rollout Checklist - Select model and lock hash. - Configure keys and rotation policy. - Integrate outbound embed at send time. - Integrate inbound verify at receive time. - Define UI badge and warning copy. - Add monitoring and audit logs. Success Metrics - Verified percentage on outbound streams. - False negative verification rate. - Reduction in phishing incidents. - Compliance audit readiness. Gmail and Outlook Implementation Notes Gmail (Google Workspace) - Outbound: use a Gmail add‑on or Apps Script that calls the embed API before send. - Inbound: add a Gmail add‑on that extracts from the message body and calls verify. - UI: show a Verified badge near the sender name and a warning if unverified. - Admin: restrict add‑on installation to approved domains and users. Outlook (Microsoft 365) - Outbound: use an Outlook add‑in (Office.js) to embed before send. - Inbound: use an Outlook add‑in or Exchange transport rule with a verification service. - UI: add a ribbon indicator or message header banner for verified senders. - Admin: deploy add‑ins centrally via Microsoft 365 admin center. Extension Monetization and Distribution (Recommended Path) Goal Monetize via an enterprise license while keeping the extension free to install. Approach - Ship the extension at no cost in the store or via managed deployment. - Access requires API tokens tied to an institutional license. - Tokens are issued and rotated by the institution’s admin. Benefits - Fits institutional procurement (annual license + support). - Avoids consumer payment friction and store policies. - Allows centralized revocation and auditability. Distribution Options - Managed deployment via Google Workspace Admin or Microsoft 365 Admin. - Private distribution for regulated environments. - Public store listing for easier discovery and trials. Phishing Simulator Test Plan Goal Validate that verified messages pass and impersonation attempts are flagged. Setup - Create a “legitimate” sender workflow that embeds provenance. - Create a “fraudulent” workflow that does not embed or uses wrong keys. Test Cases 1) Verified message, correct key Expected: Verified badge, extracted payload matches sender metadata. 2) Verified message, altered content Expected: Verification fails or tampered warning. 3) Unverified message, spoofed display name Expected: Unverified warning shown. 4) Forwarded verified message Expected: Still verifies if content intact. 5) Forwarded and edited message Expected: Verification fails or tampered warning. 6) Mixed HTML/plain text Expected: Extractor handles plaintext fallback or warns if content lost. Measurements - Verification success rate by client (web, mobile, desktop). - Time to verify (client latency). - False positives and false negatives.

Email & Social Media Deployment Guide ¶ Overview This guide explains how to use Nicrypt-Stego for email and social media content. These channels are viable, but they apply transformations (formatting, truncation, normalization) that can reduce extraction reliability. The goal is to keep payloads small, use conservative settings, and validate retrieval in the same channel you publish to. Email (Gmail and other providers) Recommended approach - Use plaintext or minimally formatted HTML. - Keep payloads short (e.g., owner + date + license). - Prefer bits_per_token=3 or 4 for short emails to reduce token count. - Use max_new_tokens with a safe margin (e.g., 400+ for MVP, 400+ for LLM tiny tests). Common transformations to watch - Line wrapping and whitespace normalization. - Signature insertion or footers. - Auto-linking (URLs, emails). - Mobile clients that reflow text. Gmail test case (end-to-end) 1) Create a stego email body Use the API to embed a short secret into a short email body: curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/provenance/embed \ -H "Authorization: Bearer test-token" \ -H "X-Scopes: provenance:embed" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"secret":"alice@example.com|2026-02-15|CC-BY-NC","cover_prompt":"Subject: Policy Update

Hello team,
Here is the updated retention policy memo for review.

Thanks,
Legal Ops","backend":"mvp","bits_per_token":3,"max_new_tokens":600}' 2) Paste the stego_text into Gmail - Compose a new email in Gmail. - Paste the returned stego_text as the email body. - Send to a test address you control. 3) Verify extraction from the received email - Copy the received email body text (avoid quoted history). - Use the verify endpoint: curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/provenance/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer test-token" \ -H "X-Scopes: provenance:verify" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"stego_text":"<PASTE_EMAIL_BODY>","backend":"mvp","bits_per_token":3,"max_new_tokens":600}' If verified, the response will include the secret. If it fails, reduce formatting, shorten the secret, or increase bits_per_token . Scripted demo (recommended) TOKEN="<JWT_BEARER>" BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1" scripts/gmail_demo.sh Verify from clipboard MODE=verify TOKEN="<JWT_BEARER>" BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1" scripts/gmail_demo.sh Verify from clipboard to file MODE=verify-clipboard TOKEN="<JWT_BEARER>" BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1" scripts/gmail_demo.sh Verify from file MODE=verify-file VERIFY_FILE="/tmp/gmail_body.txt" TOKEN="<JWT_BEARER>" BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1" scripts/gmail_demo.sh Social media Recommended approach - Keep secrets very short (e.g., owner|date|license ). - Increase bits_per_token to reduce output length. - Use the MVP backend for deterministic behavior in tests. - Expect lower reliability due to platform normalization or truncation. Platform-specific notes - X/Twitter: strict length limits; use only tiny payloads. Verification is brittle. - LinkedIn/Facebook: better for longer posts; still may normalize whitespace. - Medium/Substack: long-form posts work best for provenance embedding. Operational tips - Keep a baseline “clean” stego text in logs for comparison. - Store the original secret and model settings used. - Add a fallback verification route that allows minor edits (future robustness work).

docs.text: Gateway Integration (Exchange + Postfix) ¶ Overview This guide describes how to integrate Nicrypt‑Stego header verification into enterprise mail gateways. The target outcome is automatic verification and stamping of inbound messages using X‑Provenance headers. Common Header Set - X-Provenance-Ciphertext - X-Provenance-Model - X-Provenance-BPT - X-Provenance-Timestamp - X-Provenance-KeyId Verification Endpoint Use the API endpoint: POST /v1/provenance/verify_headers Body: { "headers": { "From": "Acme Bank alerts@yourbank.com ", "X-Provenance-Ciphertext": "gAAAAA...", "X-Provenance-Model": "sshleifer/tiny-gpt2", "X-Provenance-BPT": "4", "X-Provenance-Timestamp": "2026-02-15T12:00:00Z" } } The response includes: - verified: true|false - secret: extracted provenance - model_hash - policy: enforcement result Exchange (Microsoft 365 / On‑Prem) Option A: Transport Rule + Connector (Recommended) 1) Create a transport rule to detect messages with X‑Provenance‑Ciphertext. 2) Route those messages to a verification service (HTTP). 3) The service returns a stamp header: - X-Provenance-Verified: true|false - X-Provenance-Reason: ok|missing_provenance|not_detected 4) Exchange applies the stamp headers to the message and delivers it. Option B: Transport Agent (On‑Prem) 1) Install a custom transport agent that: - extracts the headers - calls /v1/provenance/verify_headers - stamps X‑Provenance‑Verified headers 2) Enforce policy based on apps/api/server/config/policy.yaml. Exchange Transport Rule Example (PowerShell) New-TransportRule -Name "Provenance Verify" ` -HeaderContainsMessageHeader "X-Provenance-Ciphertext" ` -HeaderContainsWords "gAAAAA" ` -SetHeaderName "X-Provenance-Verify" ` -SetHeaderValue "true" Exchange Connector + Verification Service Create a connector or transport rule to route messages to your verification service, then add headers based on the response: X-Provenance-Verified: true|false X-Provenance-Reason: ok|missing_provenance|not_detected Exchange Transport Agent Skeleton See poc/exchange_transport_agent.cs for a minimal conceptual skeleton. Exchange Agent Runbook See docs/EXCHANGE_AGENT_RUNBOOK.md for install and rollback steps. Postfix Option A: Before‑Queue Content Filter 1) Configure a content filter that reads inbound headers. 2) Call /v1/provenance/verify_headers. 3) Stamp headers and re‑inject the message. Option B: Milter 1) Create a milter that: - inspects headers - calls /v1/provenance/verify_headers - adds X‑Provenance‑Verified headers Postfix Config Example (content filter) main.cf content_filter = provfilter:127.0.0.1:2526 master.cf provfilter unix - - n - 10 smtp -o smtp_destination_concurrency_limit=10 -o smtp_send_xforward_command=yes -o disable_dns_lookups=yes -o receive_override_options=no_header_body_checks -o smtp_generic_maps= Milter Stub (header stamping) Use a milter to call /v1/provenance/verify_headers and add: X-Provenance-Verified: true|false X-Provenance-Reason: ok|missing_provenance|not_detected See poc/milter_stub.py for a minimal header stamping example. Working Milter (Postfix) See poc/postfix_milter.py (requires pymilter ). Postfix Milter Config Example main.cf smtpd_milters = unix:/var/run/provenance_milter.sock non_smtpd_milters = $smtpd_milters milter_default_action = accept milter_protocol = 6 Reference PoC Tools - poc/gateway_stamp.py reads headers from .eml and prints stamp headers. - poc/verify_headers.py reads headers and prints verification output. Operator Runbook 1) Start API and ensure JWT secrets are set. 2) Validate with a known good email (.eml). 3) Enable stamping on a pilot sender domain. 4) Monitor audit logs for verification rates and failures. 5) Roll out to additional domains. Rollback - Disable the transport rule or content filter. - Remove X‑Provenance‑Verified headers from downstream clients if needed.

Inbound (via M365 Connector) 1) Create an inbound connector that routes inbound mail to the inbound verifier host:2527. 2) Configure the connector to accept mail only from your provider IP ranges. docs.text: Institutional Rollout (One Pager) ¶ This is a high-level rollout plan for deploying Nicrypt-Stego (ns-stego) across an institution for email anti-scam provenance and (optionally) document/certificate provenance. Goal ¶ Help staff and recipients answer, reliably: - “Did this email really come from the institution?” - “Was this attachment/certificate issued by the institution and not tampered with?” What Gets Deployed ¶ API server ( nicrypt-stego-api ): org keys, verification policy, license enforcement (optional), audit logging. Email gateway (recommended): Outbound relay: adds provenance headers (attachments/certificates). Inbound stamper: adds minimal UX (“ns-stego verified”) and webmail-readable markers. Verifiers (client UX) : Gmail extension (webmail). Outlook add-in (M365). Thunderbird add-on (strongest header visibility; ideal for security/admin users). Trust Boundary (Decision Point) ¶ Choose where secrets and enforcement live: - Hosted : Nicrypt runs the API, institution deploys verifiers/gateway config. - On‑prem : institution runs the API + gateway inside its network. - Hybrid : institution keeps keys/policy on‑prem; uses hosted services for scale where acceptable. Best practice: keep keys + policy enforcement + license checks server-side. Rollout Phases ¶ Pilot (1–2 weeks) Stand up the API in a test environment. Enable gateway flow for a single internal sending identity/domain. Roll out one verifier client (typically Gmail extension) to a small group. Define “Verified / Partial / Unverified” handling guidance for staff. Production Email (2–6 weeks) Gate outbound mail through relay; stamp inbound for webmail verification. Roll out verifiers org-wide (Gmail + M365/Outlook). Turn on audit logging + monitoring dashboards. Add incident playbooks (phishing response, escalation, forensic export). Attachments and Certificates (optional, 2–8 weeks) Stamp PDFs/certificates at issuance time (API “issue certificate” workflow). Enable attachment verification in verifiers/gateway. Establish recipient-facing verification instructions and support channels. Operations Checklist (Ongoing) ¶ Key management: rotation and secure storage. Policy tuning: what to enforce vs warn; how to handle “partial”. Revocations: revoke/expire licenses (if offline SDK is distributed). Telemetry: audit logs, verification failures, upstream SMTP failures. Documentation: keep a single “How to verify” guide for users. Distribution Guidance (IP-Safe Defaults) ¶ Freely distributable: verifiers (extensions/add-ons) + docs + typed client. Controlled distribution: offline embedding SDK (license-gated, revocable). Integrator / Partner Model (e.g., Tietoevry → Nordea) ¶ Many institutions will deploy ns-stego through a systems integrator (SI) or managed service provider. Institution (the issuer / trust anchor) : Owns the sending domain(s) and brand identity. Controls org_id , allowed domains, verification policy, and cryptographic keys. Should retain continuity if vendors/operators change (key and policy ownership). Integrator (operator / implementer) : Implements and operates the API/gateway on behalf of the institution (hosted, on‑prem, or hybrid). Integrates issuing/verification into the institution’s workflows (email gateway, certificate issuance, monitoring). Operates under least-privilege service accounts and auditable access. Best practice: keep issuer identity + keys + enforcement policy institution-controlled, while allowing integrators to run infrastructure and integrations. Success Criteria ¶ Users can verify institutional messages in the primary clients (Gmail + Outlook). Attachments/certificates verify cleanly and detect tampering. Audit trail supports compliance and incident response.

docs.text: Key Management & Rotation ¶ Overview - The runtime uses ENC_PASSWORD + ENC_SALT for Nicrypt encryption. - This project supports a simple local keyring for rotation and KMS-style workflows. Keyring Settings - USE_KEYRING=1 enables loading ENC_PASSWORD/ENC_SALT from a keyring file. - KEYRING_PATH overrides the default location. - KEYRING_AUTO_CREATE=1 generates a key if none exists. - KEY_SOURCE=file + KEY_MATERIAL_PATH loads key material from a JSON file (KMS/secret sync). Licensed Offline Embed (Cyberpunk Mode) ¶ This workflow is for “offline embedding, online verification” with vendor-controlled licensing : The institution embeds provenance offline (no API calls) using the standalone SDK. The embedded payload contains a vendor-signed license token (Ed25519 / JWKS-verifiable). Anyone can verify the license token online (public key), and a verifier service can decrypt the ciphertext if it has the tenant’s Nicrypt keys. It’s a practical control/compliance lever: - If the offline SDK is abused, the payload still carries a license identity ( lic_id / jti ), and you can revoke it. Concepts ¶ 1) Vendor License Token (Ed25519) ¶ The API can mint a license token: - POST /v1/licenses/issue (requires scope licenses:issue ) - Anyone can verify the token signature: - POST /v1/licenses/verify (no auth) - GET /v1/.well-known/jwks.json (public keys) 2) Plaintext Layout (Before Nicrypt Encryption) ¶ We encrypt a plaintext that looks like: mh:<model_hash>|lic:<license_token>|<secret> mh:<model_hash>| lets verifiers detect model/config mismatch (optional but recommended). lic:<license_token>| provides vendor-controlled proof and revocation. <secret> is the human meaningful claim you want to recover at verification time. 3) Feature Gates (Recommended) ¶ License tokens can include a features object. The API can optionally enforce these: Embed flows: require one of features.embed=true or features.offline_embed=true Email signature issuance: require one of features.email_sign=true or features.signature_issue=true Step-by-Step ¶ A) Generate Vendor Keys (Ed25519) ¶ openssl genpkey -algorithm Ed25519 -out vendor_ed25519_private.pem openssl pkey -in vendor_ed25519_private.pem -pubout -out vendor_ed25519_public.pem Run the API with: export LICENSE_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$PWD/vendor_ed25519_private.pem" export LICENSE_SIGNING_PUBLIC_KEY="$PWD/vendor_ed25519_public.pem" B) Issue a License Token (Online, once per org / rotation period) ¶ TOKEN="$(JWT_SECRET=dev-secret python scripts/gen_token.py)" curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1/licenses/issue \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"days_valid":30,"features":{"offline_embed":true}}' Copy the token from the response. B2) Refresh a License Token (Online, recommended) ¶ For production, prefer short-lived tokens (e.g. 7–30 days) and refresh them on a schedule. curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1/licenses/refresh \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"token":"PASTE_OLD_TOKEN_HERE","days_valid":30}' C) Embed Offline, Keep Ciphertext (Offline) ¶ This produces: - ciphertext (store in headers / file metadata for online verification) - stego_text (innocent-looking cover text output, if you’re using LLM stego) Key idea: capacity depends on payload size, so we do: Build + encrypt payload (includes license token) Estimate needed tokens Set max_new_tokens = needed + margin Recompute model hash with final max_new_tokens , re-encrypt, then embed from nicrypt_stego.crypto import ficha from nicrypt_stego.model_hash import compute_model_hash from nicrypt_stego.bitcodec import estimated_tokens_for from nicrypt_stego.provenance import ProvenanceWriter LIC = "PASTE_LICENSE_TOKEN_HERE" secret = "alice@example.com|2026-02-19|Licensed offline embed" cover_prompt = "Subject: Test

Hello team,
This is a cover memo.
" cfg = dict( backend="mvp", model_name="sshleifer/tiny-gpt2", bits_per_token=3, device="cpu", top_k=64, redundancy=1, ecc_mode="repetition", ecc_symbols=16, ) margin = 50 # Pass 1: encrypt with a provisional max_new_tokens (only to size ciphertext) provisional_max = 300 mh1 = compute_model_hash( cfg["model_name"], cfg["backend"], cfg["bits_per_token"], provisional_max, cfg["device"], cfg["top_k"], cfg["redundancy"], cfg["ecc_mode"], cfg["ecc_symbols"], ) pt1 = f"mh:{mh1}|lic:{LIC}|{secret}" ct1 = ficha(pt1, "enc") needed = estimated_tokens_for( ct1, bits_per_token=cfg["bits_per_token"], redundancy=cfg["redundancy"], ecc_mode=cfg["ecc_mode"], ecc_symbols=cfg["ecc_symbols"], ) max_new_tokens = needed + margin # Pass 2: recompute mh with the final max_new_tokens, then re-encrypt for correctness mh2 = compute_model_hash( cfg["model_name"], cfg["backend"], cfg["bits_per_token"], max_new_tokens, cfg["device"], cfg["top_k"], cfg["redundancy"], cfg["ecc_mode"], cfg["ecc_symbols"], ) plaintext = f"mh:{mh2}|lic:{LIC}|{secret}" ciphertext = ficha(plaintext, "enc") writer = ProvenanceWriter(max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, **cfg) stego_text = writer.embed_cipher(ciphertext, cover_prompt) print("ciphertext:", ciphertext) print("stego_preview:", stego_text[:120] + "...") D) Verify Online (Ciphertext-Only) ¶ Store the ciphertext in a durable channel (examples): - Email headers: X-Provenance-Ciphertext: <ciphertext> - PDF/DOCX metadata: X-Provenance-Ciphertext - Attachment header packing: X-Provenance-Attachment: filename=...; ciphertext=...; ... Then online verification is one call: curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1/provenance/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "ciphertext":"gAAAAA...", "model_name":"sshleifer/tiny-gpt2", "bits_per_token":4 }' If you set LICENSE_REQUIRED=1 on the API, verification will only succeed if: - the decrypted plaintext includes lic:<token>|... , and - that token is valid (signature, expiry), and - it is not revoked. Revocation Storage Notes ¶ Revocations are stored by jti . For PoC, JSON file storage is fine. For higher throughput deployments, switch to SQLite and enable a small cache: export LICENSE_REVOCATIONS_BACKEND=sqlite export LICENSE_REVOCATIONS_SQLITE_PATH=/var/lib/nicrypt/revocations.sqlite export LICENSE_REVOCATIONS_CACHE_TTL_S=2.0 Practical Use Cases ¶ Institution offline pipelines : stamp documents on-prem, verify via cloud service. Edge signing : desktop apps / mail gateways embed without latency to a central API. Compliance control : every provenance claim carries a vendor-issued license identity you can revoke.

docs.text: Managed Sidecar Gateway Deployment (Customer-Hosted) ¶ This is the “gateway as a service” operating model that matches what we tested locally, but deployed inside a customer environment (on‑prem or customer VPC). Nicrypt (or an integrator) can operate it, while the customer keeps data inside their perimeter. What “Sidecar” Means Here ¶ The customer hosts the gateway runtime (VM(s) or Kubernetes) in their environment. The gateway relays mail only inside customer-controlled network paths. The gateway forwards to the customer’s chosen upstream (M365, Gmail/Workspace, Brevo/SES, Postfix, etc.). Components ¶ Outbound relay (injector) : accepts SMTP from the customer’s sending systems and injects attachment provenance headers. Local port (default): 2525 Inbound stamper (verifier/stamper) : receives the relayed message, stamps minimal UX (“ns-stego verified”) + machine markers for webmail verifiers, then forwards upstream. Local port (default): 2527 API server ( nicrypt-stego-api ): keys, verification, signature issuance, policy, audit. Local port (example): 8125 High-Level Flow ¶ flowchart LR A[Customer apps / MTA] -->|SMTP| R[Outbound relay :2525] R -->|SMTP| S[Inbound stamper :2527] S -->|SMTP| U[Upstream provider\n(M365 / Workspace / Brevo / Postfix)] S -->|HTTP| API[nicrypt-stego-api :8125] R -->|HTTP (optional)| API Notes: - The Gmail verifier extension can’t read message headers, so the inbound stamper must ensure the verification markers are present in the body in a Gmail-resilient way. - The API should be reachable from the gateway over the customer network (prefer private IPs). Network & Ports ¶ Minimum (pilot): - 2525/tcp inbound from customer send path → outbound relay - 2527/tcp inbound from outbound relay → inbound stamper (same host or internal network) - 8125/tcp inbound stamper → API ( /v1/... ) Recommended: - Bind SMTP listeners to private interfaces only (no public exposure). - Allow-list sender IPs / subnets for 2525 and 2527 . Security Posture (Recommended Defaults) ¶ SMTP hop security (pick one, strongest first): 1. mTLS between customer MTA and gateway, plus IP allow-lists 2. VPN / private peering + IP allow-lists 3. SMTP AUTH on the relay hop (least preferred in enterprise) API security: - Use a least-privilege API token for the gateway. - Prefer file-based secrets (e.g., API_TOKEN_PATH , PROVENANCE_LICENSE_TOKEN_PATH ) instead of environment literals. - Enable audit logging and forward logs to the customer SIEM if required. Deployment Options ¶ Option A: VM + systemd (Linux) ¶ Deploy nicrypt-stego-api + gateway daemons on a hardened VM. Install services via the repo’s systemd targets and set environment via /etc/... or systemd drop-ins. Reference: docs/WINDOWS_SERVICE_RUNBOOK.md (concept), docs/GATEWAY_INTEGRATION.md (flow). Option B: Kubernetes (customer VPC / on‑prem) ¶ Run 3 Deployments: API ( nicrypt-stego-api ) relay ( smtp_relay.py ) stamper ( smtp_inbound_daemon.py ) Put SMTP behind an internal LoadBalancer / ClusterIP + an internal TCP ingress (depending on platform). Use Kubernetes Secrets for API tokens and upstream SMTP credentials. SMTP Provider Integration (Where You “Point Mail Flow”) ¶ Common patterns: - M365 : connectors/rules route outbound (and optionally inbound) through the sidecar gateway. - Reference: docs/EXCHANGE_AGENT_RUNBOOK.md , docs/EMAIL_GATEWAY_FLOW.md - Postfix : relayhost for outbound, content_filter for inbound stamping. - Reference: docs/GATEWAY_INTEGRATION.md - SMTP provider (Brevo/SES/Sendgrid) : gateway forwards upstream using provider credentials. Deliverability best practice: - Avoid having the gateway be the final public sender if it would break SPF/DKIM alignment. - Prefer forwarding to the customer’s official sending provider so DKIM/SPF remain consistent. Operations Checklist ¶ Before pilot: - Confirm SMTP forwarding works end-to-end (relay → stamper → upstream). - Confirm provenance verify works (Gmail + Thunderbird verifiers). - Confirm queue/retry behavior is acceptable (transient upstream failures). - Confirm no secrets are logged. During production: - Monitor: - upstream SMTP auth failures - queue depth / retry counts - verification failures (policy: missing_provenance, license_missing, etc.) - Rotate: - API JWT secrets / signing keys per policy - SMTP creds (provider rotation) - Incident response: - export audit logs - snapshot gateway config and versions (git SHA / package build-info) Smoke Test (Operator) ¶ On the gateway host (or operator bastion): make gateway-status Then send a test message through the relay and verify it using: - Gmail extension (recipient experience) - Thunderbird add-on (admin/security experience) Related Docs ¶ docs/EMAIL_GATEWAY_FLOW.md (quick sheet, ports, flow) docs/GATEWAY_ONLY_MANUAL.md (manual operation) docs/GATEWAY_INTEGRATION.md (Exchange/Postfix integration) docs/PRODUCTION_WORKFLOW.md and docs/PRODUCTION_READINESS.md (hardening)

docs.text: Monetization and Institutional Implementation ¶ Purpose This document describes how an institution can implement Nicrypt-Stego and how the product can be monetized in a predictable, enterprise-friendly way. Executive Summary Nicrypt-Stego is best deployed as an on‑prem or private‑cloud provenance service that embeds encrypted provenance into text and verifies it later. Institutions pay for the reduction of compliance risk, the ability to prove authorship, and the operational savings from automated verification. Monetization should align to institutional procurement norms: annual licensing, support tiers, and optional usage‑based overages. Institutional Implementation Architecture Pattern Central Provenance Service: Deploy the API behind the institution’s firewall with authenticated service tokens. Integration Points: Connect document creation, email, LMS, CMS, and research portals to embed on publish and verify on intake. Audit Pipeline: Forward verification logs to SIEM or audit storage. Integrator / Partner Model (Systems Integrators) Many enterprise buyers will use a systems integrator (SI) or managed service provider to deploy and operate ns-stego. Institution as issuer: Owns the org_id , keys, and verification policy (the trust anchor). Approves allowed sending domains and enforcement posture. Integrator as operator: Runs deployments (on‑prem/private cloud/hybrid) and integrates workflows (gateway, issuance, monitoring). Uses least‑privilege service credentials, with all privileged actions audited. Commercial structure options: - Reseller / referral partner margin (SI sells the subscription to the institution). - Managed service add‑on (SI bundles ns-stego into an operational offering). - NFR + training licenses for SI development/testing environments. Deployment Options On‑prem: Best for regulated data, with internal model hosting and no external calls. Private cloud: Suitable when the institution already has a secure cloud footprint. Workflow Integration Authoring systems: Embed provenance at the point of approval or export. Receiving systems: Verify on upload or view to detect tampering or unsigned content. Governance: Maintain key rotation policies and a model registry for stable verification. Key Management and Compliance Use keys:manage and keys:read endpoints to rotate and audit provenance keys. Store keys in an institution‑managed vault and restrict decrypt capability. Record model hash + key id in logs for non‑repudiation. Success Criteria Provenance is embedded for all official communications. Verification is enforced at ingestion points. Audit trail supports internal and external compliance reviews. Monetization Model Annual License (Recommended for Institutions) Base license based on institution size and deployment nodes. Includes core API, on‑prem deployment, and standard support. Add‑ons for high‑availability, custom integrations, or model hosting. Usage‑Based Overage Included volume per year, with overages per embedded or verified document. Useful for large universities with variable seasonal usage. Enterprise Support and SLA Priority response, security reviews, and compliance documentation. Dedicated onboarding and integration assistance. Pricing Dimensions (Non‑Exhaustive) - Number of systems integrated. - Total documents and emails processed per year. - Number of environments and nodes. - Support tier and SLA. Business Value to Institutions - Compliance assurance: cryptographic proof of origin. - Risk reduction: detection of forged or altered content. - Operational efficiency: reduced manual verification and disputes. - Trust at scale: consistent provenance across communications. Implementation Roadmap Phase 1: Pilot - Integrate with a single authoritative channel such as legal or compliance memos. - Measure verification success and audit coverage. Phase 2: Expansion - Add email announcements, LMS materials, and research outputs. - Enable verification at intake points and monitor false positives. Phase 3: Institution‑wide - Standardize provenance across departments. - Formalize key rotation and retention policies. Operational Checklist - Define permitted models and lock model hash. - Configure JWT issuance and scope policies. - Enable logging and data retention policies. - Establish key rotation cadence and recovery plan. Risks and Mitigations - Model drift: lock model versions and record model hashes. - Access control: restrict decrypt scope to authorized services. - Content changes: handle truncated text with redundancy or ECC. docs.text: Pilot: Local Gateway Test Guide (Customer Premises) ¶ This guide is the step-by-step “runbook” for a pilot deployment on a customer machine/network where you want to validate the full email + attachment provenance loop : SMTP relay ( 2525 ) injects provenance for attachments/certificates. SMTP inbound stamper ( 2527 ) stamps minimal UX markers for verifiers (Gmail/Thunderbird). ns-stego API ( 8125 ) provides verification and signature issuance. Gmail extension / Thunderbird add-on verify what recipients see. Assumptions: - You are running from the repo root: ns-stego/ - You have Python 3.11 and the project venv set up ( .venv/ ) - You have working upstream SMTP credentials (Brevo/SES/M365 relay, etc.) - You can receive mail in Gmail and/or Thunderbird. 0) Environment Variables (What + Where) ¶ Where to store env vars ¶ Repo defaults: .env.example (placeholders only; treated as defaults) Your real values: .env (overrides .env.example ) Do not put real secrets into .env.example . Variables used by the gateway ¶ API connectivity (used by both relay + inbound stamper): - API_BASE - Example: http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 - What it does: points the gateway to the ns-stego API. - API_TOKEN (or API_TOKEN_PATH ) - What it does: JWT used by the gateway to call API endpoints. - Recommended: use API_TOKEN_PATH to avoid fragile long env values. Upstream SMTP (used by inbound stamper to forward to the real world): - INBOUND_SMTP_HOST / INBOUND_SMTP_PORT - INBOUND_SMTP_USER / INBOUND_SMTP_PASS - What it does: credentials to your upstream SMTP provider (Brevo, SES, etc.) Relay -> Stamper hop (used by relay to forward locally): - SMTP_HOST / SMTP_PORT - Typical: SMTP_HOST=127.0.0.1 , SMTP_PORT=2527 Provenance stamping: - STAMP_BODY (default 1 ) - If 1 , inbound stamper adds visible “ns-stego verified” badge and machine markers. - PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENTS (default 1 ) - If 1 , gateway emits attachment provenance markers for each attachment. - PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENT_MODE - Typical: metadata (best for certificate verification UX) - Other: hash (smaller marker; “tamper detect” only) License enforcement (recommended for pilots that test licensing): - PROVENANCE_LICENSE_TOKEN_PATH - File containing a vendor license JWT. - Used when license enforcement is enabled on the API. Minimal .env template (pilot) ¶ Create/edit .env : API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 # Gateway calls to the API (prefer path form) API_TOKEN_PATH=/tmp/api_token.jwt # Relay forwards locally to inbound stamper SMTP_HOST=127.0.0.1 SMTP_PORT=2527 # Inbound stamper forwards to upstream SMTP provider INBOUND_SMTP_HOST=smtp-relay.brevo.com INBOUND_SMTP_PORT=587 INBOUND_SMTP_USER=your-smtp-login INBOUND_SMTP_PASS=your-smtp-key # Stamping behavior STAMP_BODY=1 PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENTS=1 PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENT_MODE=metadata # License token (file) PROVENANCE_LICENSE_TOKEN_PATH=/tmp/provenance_license.jwt 1) Ensure the API token has required scopes (or generate one) ¶ The pilot typically needs a token that can: - verify provenance ( provenance:verify ) - verify attachment headers ( provenance:verify ) - issue compact signature tokens for Gmail marker strategy ( signature:issue and/or signature:verify ) - issue certificates (if you do step 6) ( certificates:issue ) - (optional) manage keys / licenses Generate a dev token (local pilot) ¶ If your API uses JWT_SECRET locally: . .venv/bin/activate export JWT_SECRET=dev-secret python scripts/gen_token.py > /tmp/api_token.jwt If you want to eyeball it: head -c 32 /tmp/api_token.jwt && echo Note: - In production, the institution will have their own signing secret / issuer and issuance process. For pilots, a dev token is acceptable. 2) Save API token into the token file ¶ Recommended file (used by gateway installers and scripts): - /tmp/api_token.jwt If you generated it in step 1, you’re already done. 3) Ensure you have a valid vendor license token (or issue one) ¶ When the API is configured to require licenses for certain verification/issuance flows, you must provide a license token to the gateway (path recommended). Save license token to file ¶ Recommended file: - /tmp/provenance_license.jwt Example: printf '%s' "$LICENSE_TOKEN" > /tmp/provenance_license.jwt chmod 600 /tmp/provenance_license.jwt Issue a license token (API route) ¶ If your API exposes a license issuance endpoint (admin-scoped), issue via curl: API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 API_TOKEN="$(cat /tmp/api_token.jwt)" curl -sS -X POST "$API_BASE/licenses/issue" \\ -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\ -d '{ "org_id":"public", "lic_id":"lic_demo", "features":{"offline_embed":true,"signature_issue":true}, "ttl_seconds":3600 }' | tee /tmp/license_issue.json Then extract and store the returned license_token : python3 - <<'PY' import json data=json.load(open('/tmp/license_issue.json','r')) print(data.get('license_token','')) PY Save it: python3 - <<'PY' import json, os data=json.load(open('/tmp/license_issue.json','r')) t=data.get('license_token','') if not t: raise SystemExit('no license_token in response') open('/tmp/provenance_license.jwt','w').write(t) print('wrote /tmp/provenance_license.jwt') PY chmod 600 /tmp/provenance_license.jwt 4) Install and start the gateway services (relay + inbound) ¶ This installs service definitions (launchd on macOS, systemd on Linux), enables them, and starts them. macOS (launchd): make install-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make enable-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make start-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 Linux (systemd): make install-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make enable-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make start-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 Tip: - make restart-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 is the “do the right thing” idempotent target on macOS. 5) Confirm the gateway is healthy ¶ Check listeners and health: make gateway-status ENABLE_IMAP=0 Expected: - Port 2525 listening (relay) - Port 2527 listening (inbound stamper) - Inbound health endpoint returns JSON (may briefly “not ready” right after restart) If emails aren’t sending: - Check inbound SMTP auth: tail -n 200 /tmp/nicrypt-inbound.err Confirm launchd/systemd is using real upstream creds: UID=$(id -u) launchctl print "gui/$UID/com.nicrypt.gateway.inbound" | grep -A6 INBOUND_SMTP_ 2>/dev/null || true 6) Stamp (issue) a certificate / PDF you will attach ¶ This creates a stamped PDF that carries hidden provenance. Example: TOKEN="$(cat /tmp/api_token.jwt)" LICENSE_TOKEN="$(cat /tmp/provenance_license.jwt)" python scripts/issue_certificate.py \\ --api-base http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 \\ --api-token "$TOKEN" \\ --license-token "$LICENSE_TOKEN" \\ --in docs/CoverLetterBinance.pdf \\ --out /tmp/pilot_stamped.pdf \\ --issuer-id "uni:example" \\ --cert-id "cert:pilot-001" \\ --recipient-id "person:alice" \\ --secret "person:alice" Sanity check verification (local API): python scripts/verify_certificate.py \\ --api-base http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 \\ --api-token "$TOKEN" \\ --in /tmp/pilot_stamped.pdf 7) Activate verifiers (Gmail extension / Thunderbird add-on) ¶ Gmail extension (Chrome) ¶ Install packaged artifact: dist/addons/gmail-extension.zip Chrome: chrome://extensions Enable “Developer mode” “Load unpacked”: unzip gmail-extension.zip to a folder select that folder (contains manifest.json ) Open extension Options and set: Base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 (pilot/local) Token: leave blank for public verify, or paste your JWT if your verify requires it Thunderbird add-on ¶ Install: dist/addons/thunderbird-addon.xpi Thunderbird → Add-ons and Themes → gear icon → “Install Add-on From File…” Set in add-on settings: API Base: http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 API Token: $(cat /tmp/api_token.jwt) (Thunderbird can read headers; token often used in pilots) 8) Send an email with the stamped attachment and verify it ¶ Send through the relay so the gateway can inject/stamp: python3 scripts/send_signed_attachment.py \\ --mail-to your.recipient@example.com \\ --attach /tmp/pilot_stamped.pdf \\ --qa-id "pilot-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)" \\ --save-eml /tmp/nicrypt-last.eml \\ --api-token "$(cat /tmp/api_token.jwt)" \\ --license-token-path /tmp/provenance_license.jwt Local verify of the generated .eml (before it hits the outside world): python scripts/verify_email.py /tmp/nicrypt-last.eml \\ --api-base http://127.0.0.1:8125/v1 \\ --api-token "$(cat /tmp/api_token.jwt)" \\ --verdict Then verify in the recipient client: - Gmail: open the email → click “Verify provenance” → expect “Verified sender” + attachments verified. - Thunderbird: open the email → click “Verify provenance” → expect sender + attachment verification. Troubleshooting (Fast) ¶ Gateway sends but upstream rejects (SMTP 535 auth): - Verify INBOUND_SMTP_USER/INBOUND_SMTP_PASS in .env - Restart services: make restart-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 Gmail says “No provenance markers”: - Ensure STAMP_BODY=1 - Ensure inbound stamper is in the path (relay → inbound → upstream) - Ensure your message body includes the minimal marker badge (ns-stego verified) Attachment shows unverified: - Ensure PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENTS=1 - Ensure PROVENANCE_ATTACHMENT_MODE=metadata for certificate-style flows - Confirm license token is valid/not expired (if required)

docs.text: Nicrypt-Stego — Verifiable Origin for Text Content (Enterprise Focus) ¶ One-liner Cryptographic provenance embedded inside normal-looking text, enabling enterprises to prove origin, detect tampering, and meet compliance without changing workflows. Problem Enterprises cannot reliably prove the origin of AI-generated or human-authored text once it leaves the system. This creates legal exposure, audit gaps, and IP disputes. Solution Nicrypt-Stego embeds encrypted provenance directly into text. Outputs look normal, publish anywhere, and remain verifiable using an internal key. Why now AI content is everywhere, but provenance and accountability are weak. Enterprises need audit-ready evidence, not probabilistic watermarking. Differentiators - Cryptographic proof vs heuristic watermarking - Works with on-prem models and private data - Deterministic verification with model and config hashes Business impact - Reduce compliance risk for regulated documentation - Protect IP in reports, research, and corporate comms - Establish defensible authorship trails for AI outputs - Extend trust to attachments: sign letters/contracts before send so recipients can verify files before opening. Primary users - Legal and compliance teams - Security and governance leaders - Engineering teams shipping AI workflows Go-to-market SDKs for product teams, CLI for compliance/legal workflows, and integrations for CMS/document pipelines. Pricing hooks Per-seat compliance tooling, per-call API usage, and enterprise platform licensing. Buyer model: businesses pay to sign outbound communications; their customers verify with free client extensions/add-ins. Call to action Pilot in one compliance-critical workflow and expand to enterprise content pipelines.

docs.text: Privacy Policy: ns-stego Gmail Extension ¶ Last updated: 2026-02-26 Summary ¶ The ns-stego Gmail extension helps users verify whether an email and/or its attachments include valid ns-stego provenance markers . The extension only processes the currently opened Gmail message to extract verification markers and then calls a user-configured verification API to validate them. Data We Access ¶ When you click Verify provenance (and when any auto-verify/auto-sign features are enabled), the extension may access: - The content of the currently opened Gmail message (message body text and rendered HTML) to find ns-stego markers (for example: NS-SIG-LINK , NS-ATTB64 , and related provenance markers). - The sender address and related provenance metadata if present in markers. Data We Send ¶ The extension sends only the minimum necessary verification material to your configured verification API endpoint, such as: - A signature token (for example: ns_sig=... ) - A ciphertext/marker payload (for example: NS-ATTB64: ... ) - Minimal parameters required by the verification endpoint The extension does not intentionally send your full email content to the API. Data We Store ¶ The extension stores configuration in Chrome Sync storage: - Verification API base URL - API token (if you choose to use one) - Non-sensitive preferences (toggles and UI settings) Data We Do Not Sell or Use for Ads ¶ We do not sell personal data. We do not run ads. We do not use email content for training or profiling. We do not intentionally collect inbox history. Security Notes ¶ Use an HTTPS verification API base URL whenever possible. Treat API tokens as secrets. If your deployment is recipient-facing, prefer a verification mode that does not require end users to paste privileged tokens. Third Parties ¶ Verification is performed by the verification API you configure. Your institution may operate this API, or it may be operated by a hosting provider. This policy does not cover how that API stores or processes data beyond what is described here. Contact ¶ For support or privacy questions, contact: support@your-domain.example .

docs.text: Production Readiness Checklist ¶ Technical protection - See docs/TECHNICAL_PROTECTION_CHECKLIST.md for license enforcement, scope gating, and abuse controls. Priority 1 (Security + Trust) - Key management + rotation (KMS/HSM optional). - Per-tenant key isolation (org_id scoping). - Policy enforcement in API + gateway flows. - Auditable provenance logs (append-only, signed, exportable). Priority 2 (Reliability + Scale) - Queue + retry for SMTP/IMAP flows. - Rate limits and backpressure. - Dead-letter queue for failures. - Idempotency for embed/verify jobs. - Per-endpoint quotas per org (embed/verify). Priority 4 (Client UX) - Header-based badges (Gmail/Outlook). - Admin dashboard (verification stats, failure drilldowns). - End-user explainers for verified/unverified. Priority 5 (Compliance + Legal) - Retention policies and deletion windows. - PII handling and redaction. - DPIA template for institutions. - Per-org provenance storage separation (when enabling persistence). docs.text: Production Workflow: Email Provenance ¶ Overview Production deployments should avoid relying on email body steganography in consumer clients. Use SMTP header injection for outbound mail and header verification on inbound mail. Certificate provenance For institutional certificates (PDFs), see docs/CERTIFICATE_PROVENANCE_SPRINT.md . Email vs Certificate Provenance (Quick Comparison) See docs/EMAIL_VS_CERTIFICATE_COMPARISON.md . Outbound (Signing) 1. Email is created in the organization’s mail system. 2. SMTP relay injects provenance headers: - X-Provenance-Ciphertext - X-Provenance-Model - X-Provenance-BPT - X-Provenance-Timestamp - X-Provenance-KeyId 3. Email is delivered without modifying the visible body. Inbound (Verification) 1. Mail gateway or client reads provenance headers. 2. Verify via /v1/provenance/verify_headers . 3. UI displays Verified/Unverified badge. Gateway Stamp (PoC) Use poc/gateway_stamp.py to turn inbound headers into verification headers: python poc/gateway_stamp.py /path/to/message.eml Example output headers: X-Provenance-Verified: true X-Provenance-Reason: ok X-Provenance-Model-Hash: mhash_... X-Provenance-Timestamp: 2026-02-15T... Policy Enforcement Use apps/api/server/config/policy.yaml to enforce which sender domains must include provenance. Example required_sender_domains: - veriforensic.com allow_missing_provenance: false PoC Tools - poc/smtp_sender.py for direct SMTP sending with headers. - poc/smtp_relay.py as a lightweight header‑injecting relay. - poc/verify_headers.py for verifying .eml files. Operational Checklist - Rotate keys and keep key ids in headers. - Lock model hashes for stable verification. - Enable audit logging for header verification. Daemon Config - poc/daemon_config.env for inbound verifier settings. - poc/nicrypt-*.service legacy templates (deprecated; do not copy as-is). - scripts/systemd_render.py renders correct systemd unit files for the current repo root. Install systemd service (example) make install-services ENABLE_IMAP=1 make enable-services ENABLE_IMAP=1 make start-services ENABLE_IMAP=1 make status-services ENABLE_IMAP=1 Outbound relay systemd (example) make install-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make enable-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make start-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 make status-services ENABLE_IMAP=0 systemd override example sudo systemctl edit nicrypt-inbound.service Then add: [Service] Environment="STAMP_BODY=1" Environment="INBOUND_SMTP_PORT=587" Outbound override example sudo systemctl edit nicrypt-outbound.service Then add: [Service] Environment="SMTP_PORT=587" IMAP override example sudo systemctl edit nicrypt-imap.service Then add: [Service] Environment="IMAP_HOST=mail.privateemail.com" Environment="IMAP_USE_KEYWORDS=1" IMAP Watcher Report Run with --report to print per-cycle totals: python poc/imap_watcher.py --report IMAP Watcher Health Default health endpoint on 127.0.0.1:8100 (configurable via IMAP_HEALTH_PORT ). IMAP Watcher Options - --all to process all messages (not just UNSEEN) - --label-only to avoid moving messages - --audit-log /path/file.jsonl to append JSONL audit records launchd log override (macOS) Edit the plist to change log paths: ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.nicrypt.imap.plist

docs.text: Provenance Store (Org-Scoped) ¶ Overview - The provenance store is an optional append-only JSONL log for embedded/verified events. - It is useful for audit trails, compliance exports, and incident response. - Events are scoped per org_id when partitioning is enabled. Environment variables - PROVENANCE_STORE_ENABLED=1 - PROVENANCE_STORE_PATH=/var/log/nicrypt/provenance.jsonl - PROVENANCE_STORE_PARTITION=1 Partitioning rules - If PROVENANCE_STORE_PARTITION=1, logs are written per org_id. - If PROVENANCE_STORE_PATH is a directory, files are named provenance_<org_id>.jsonl . - If PROVENANCE_STORE_PATH is a file, the org_id is appended to the filename. Sample event { "ts": "2026-02-15T22:21:00.000000+00:00", "org_id": "org_a", "request_id": "req_abc123", "event": "embed", "model_name": "sshleifer/tiny-gpt2", "model_hash": "mhash_123456", "payload_bytes": 42 }

docs.text: Nicrypt-Stego: Cryptographic Provenance via LLM Steganography ¶ Software Specification Document Version: 0.1.0 (Draft) Date: 2026-02-12 Authors: Derived from research insights and the Nicrypt encryption package. Introduction In the current era, every piece of text published online is liable to be scraped, ingested, and memorized by large language models (LLMs). Once data enters a model’s weights, it cannot be reliably removed, and the original author loses all control and attribution. Traditional digital signatures or watermarks are easily stripped during scraping, and post-hoc authorship claims rely on non‑cryptographic stylometry. Nicrypt-Stego solves this problem by combining symmetric encryption with LLM‑based steganography. It allows an author to: Encrypt a secret provenance message (e.g., author identity, timestamp, copyright notice) using the existing Nicrypt library. Embed the resulting ciphertext into an innocuous, human‑readable cover text using token‑level steganography performed by a local LLM. Publish the steganographic text anywhere (web, social media, PDFs). Later recover the ciphertext from the published text and decrypt it, providing cryptographic proof of authorship. This specification describes the architecture, components, and API for the nicrypt-stego Python package, which extends Nicrypt with state‑of‑the‑art steganographic embedding and extraction routines. Background & Related Work Research Contribution ExpShield (NDSS 2026) Proactive defense via invisible perturbations; demonstrates that data owners can prevent memorization. LLMs‑can‑hide‑text (ACL 2025) First practical method to embed secret bits into LLM‑generated text while preserving fluency and length. Infusion (ICLR 2026) Poisoning via influence‑function guided edits; shows that very few modified samples can control model behaviour. TrajPrint (S&P 2026) Lossless model fingerprinting using decodable watermarks. Nicrypt‑Stego draws directly from LLMs‑can‑hide‑text: we use its token‑selection algorithm to encode arbitrary binary data (ciphertext) into natural language. Unlike prior work that focuses on hiding plaintext secrets, we hide encrypted payloads, enabling asymmetric verification – only the key holder can prove origin. Objectives Provide a simple, pip‑installable Python library that integrates Nicrypt encryption with LLM‑based steganography. Achieve cryptographic authorship verification: the ability to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that a given text was authored by the holder of a secret key. Maintain output text quality: steganographic cover texts must be grammatically correct, topically relevant, and indistinguishable from normal human‑written text. Minimize computational overhead: use small, locally runnable open‑source LLMs (e.g., Llama‑3‑8B, Mistral‑7B) so that no API calls are required. Support arbitrary binary ciphertext produced by Nicrypt (Fernet tokens, base64‑encoded). TLS: - Only allow NS_STEGO_API_BASE over HTTPS in production environments. Integration tests: use small local models (e.g., "gpt2") to test full protect/verify cycles. Fluency evaluation: compute perplexity of stego texts vs. unconstrained generation; aim for <10% degradation. Capacity benchmarks: measure maximum embeddable bytes for different bit‑per‑token settings. Model‑dependent Develop a calibration technique to make bin assignments model‑agnostic. Only text output Extend to other modalities (code, structured data). Manual key management Integrate with hardware security modules or cloud KMS. Conclusion Nicrypt‑Stego transforms a simple symmetric encryption utility into a complete cryptographic provenance system. By leveraging recent advances in LLM steganography, it offers the first practical, developer‑friendly tool for proving authorship in the age of ubiquitous AI training. The specification above is immediately actionable; all components are either already implemented (Nicrypt) or have public research implementations (token‑level steganography). The remaining work is integration, packaging, and user‑experience refinement. Next steps: Fork / reference an existing open‑source implementation of LLM steganography. Build the nicrypt_stego package with the API described. Write extensive documentation and publish on PyPI. Release as open‑source under a permissive license (MIT). Recommended paid routes: 1) Embed provenance (paid) - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/embed - Upstream: POST {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/provenance/embed_cipher 2) Issue certificate/PDF (paid) - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/certificates/issue - Upstream: POST {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/certificates/issue 3) Issue signature token (paid) - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/signature/issue - Upstream: POST {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/signature/issue (or /signature/token ) 4) Keys management (paid/admin) - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/keys/create -> {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/keys - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/keys/rotate -> {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/keys/{key_id}/rotate - SaaS: GET /api/v1/ns-stego/keys/list -> {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/keys 5) Licensing (paid/admin) - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/licenses/issue -> {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/licenses/issue - SaaS: POST /api/v1/ns-stego/licenses/revoke -> {NS_STEGO_API_BASE}/licenses/revoke 11.6 Subscription and Billing Strategy (Verify Free) Recommended enforcement: - Public verify endpoints: free, rate-limited. - Issuance/admin endpoints: require subscription plan + enforce per-feature entitlements. Typical metering units: - per embed call - per certificate issued - per signature issued - per key rotation / key creation - per license issued/revoked 11.7 Security Hygiene Secrets: - Never accept ns-stego service tokens from browsers; keep them server-side. - Prefer file-based secrets in deployments where possible. - Ensure logs never include API tokens or license tokens. TLS: - Only allow NS_STEGO_API_BASE over HTTPS in production environments. Auditing: - Store request_id returned by ns-stego for traceability across services. pip install nicrypt-stego Additionally, the user must install PyTorch (instructions vary by platform) and have access to the chosen LLM (downloaded via Hugging Face). Environment variables (as required by Nicrypt): bash export ENC_KEY='your-32-byte-base64-key' export ENC_SALT='your-16-byte-base64-salt' 11. Testing Strategy Unit tests: verify that embed_cipher(extract_cipher(text)) == cipher for random ciphertexts. Integration tests: use small local models (e.g., "gpt2") to test full protect/verify cycles. Fluency evaluation: compute perplexity of stego texts vs. unconstrained generation; aim for <10% degradation. Capacity benchmarks: measure maximum embeddable bytes for different bit‑per‑token settings. Limitations and Future Work Limitation Planned Enhancement Fragile to editing Integrate error‑correcting codes (Reed–Solomon) and redundant embedding. Model‑dependent Develop a calibration technique to make bin assignments model‑agnostic. Only text output Extend to other modalities (code, structured data). Manual key management Integrate with hardware security modules or cloud KMS. Conclusion Nicrypt‑Stego transforms a simple symmetric encryption utility into a complete cryptographic provenance system. By leveraging recent advances in LLM steganography, it offers the first practical, developer‑friendly tool for proving authorship in the age of ubiquitous AI training. The specification above is immediately actionable; all components are either already implemented (Nicrypt) or have public research implementations (token‑level steganography). The remaining work is integration, packaging, and user‑experience refinement. Next steps: Fork / reference an existing open‑source implementation of LLM steganography. Build the nicrypt_stego package with the API described. Write extensive documentation and publish on PyPI. Release as open‑source under a permissive license (MIT). This specification is derived from a research‑backed analysis of the 2026 AI provenance landscape and the existing Nicrypt encryption library.

docs.text: Technical Protection Checklist (SDK) ¶ Scope This checklist focuses on technical enforcement and operational controls that protect SDK use and prevent unauthorized embedding or signing. Identity and Licensing - [x] License validation enforced at API boundary (via LICENSE_REQUIRED=1 ). - [x] License expiry/renewal path implemented ( /v1/licenses/issue with exp ) and tested. - [x] Capability tokens (time-boxed) issued per org + scope (license token includes org_id + features + exp). - [x] Token revocation path implemented and tested ( /v1/licenses/revoke by jti ). - [x] Public key distribution implemented (JWKS: /v1/.well-known/jwks.json ). - [x] Offline embed pattern documented (see docs/LICENSED_OFFLINE_EMBED.md ). - [x] Optional embed/sign boundary enforcement ( LICENSE_REQUIRED_FOR_EMBED=1 , LICENSE_REQUIRED_FOR_SIGNATURE=1 ). - [x] License token binding enforced (token org_id must match request org_id ; features gates per operation). - [x] License renewal path implemented ( /v1/licenses/refresh ) and tested. - [x] Revocation storage hardened (JSON or SQLite backend + small TTL cache). - [x] License lifecycle events audited (issue/refresh/revoke recorded in provenance store when enabled). - [x] Swagger/OpenAPI examples include org_id / lic_id / ttl_seconds for license issuance and include license_token on embed/sign examples for easy manual testing. Auth and Scope Enforcement - [ ] All embed/sign endpoints require scopes (provenance:embed, signature:issue). - [ ] Verify endpoints remain accessible with least-privilege scopes. - [ ] Per-org policy enforcement (sender domains, required provenance). - [ ] API rejects missing/invalid org_id in multi-tenant mode. Server-Side IP Protection - [ ] Core embedding/quality logic stays server-side (thin clients). - [ ] Model hash and capacity checks enforced server-side. - [ ] Request/response schemas do not leak secrets or key material. Key Management - [ ] Key source selectable (env, file, KMS). - [ ] Rotation procedure documented and automated. - [ ] Key usage is logged (audit trail). - [ ] Decryption fails cleanly on key mismatch. Telemetry and Auditing - [ ] Structured logs include org_id + request_id + endpoint. - [ ] Audit log records embed/sign/verify actions. - [ ] Retention + export policies documented. Rate Limits and Abuse Controls - [ ] Per-org throughput limits (embed/verify/sign). - [ ] Burst control and backpressure configured. - [ ] Invalid token attempts rate-limited. Client UX Protections - [ ] Verified badge shown only on server-verified status. - [ ] “Partial” status when attachments fail verification. - [ ] No local-only verification claims. Gateway Protections - [ ] Relay→inbound chain enforced (stamp body for Gmail). - [ ] Attachment header stamping enabled for outbound. - [ ] SMTP STARTTLS behavior correct for local hop. Deployment Hardening - [ ] Service env vars sourced securely (not hardcoded). - [ ] Health endpoints available for monitoring. - [ ] CI verifies enforcement paths (license + scopes).

docs.text: Scope This checklist focuses on technical enforcement and operational controls that protect SDK use and prevent unauthorized embedding or signing. Identity and Licensing - [x] License validation enforced at API boundary (via LICENSE_REQUIRED=1 ). - [x] License expiry/renewal path implemented ( /v1/licenses/issue with exp ) and tested. - [x] Capability tokens (time-boxed) issued per org + scope (license token includes org_id + features + exp). - [x] Token revocation path implemented and tested ( /v1/licenses/revoke by jti ). - [x] Public key distribution implemented (JWKS: /v1/.well-known/jwks.json ). - [x] Offline embed pattern documented (see docs/LICENSED_OFFLINE_EMBED.md ). - [x] Optional embed/sign boundary enforcement ( LICENSE_REQUIRED_FOR_EMBED=1 , LICENSE_REQUIRED_FOR_SIGNATURE=1 ). - [x] License token binding enforced (token org_id must match request org_id ; features gates per operation). - [x] License renewal path implemented ( /v1/licenses/refresh ) and tested. - [x] Revocation storage hardened (JSON or SQLite backend + small TTL cache). - [x] License lifecycle events audited (issue/refresh/revoke recorded in provenance store when enabled). - [x] Swagger/OpenAPI examples include org_id / lic_id / ttl_seconds for license issuance and include license_token on embed/sign examples for easy manual testing. Auth and Scope Enforcement - [ ] All embed/sign endpoints require scopes (provenance:embed, signature:issue). - [ ] Verify endpoints remain accessible with least-privilege scopes. - [ ] Per-org policy enforcement (sender domains, required provenance). - [ ] API rejects missing/invalid org_id in multi-tenant mode. Server-Side IP Protection - [ ] Core embedding/quality logic stays server-side (thin clients). - [ ] Model hash and capacity checks enforced server-side. - [ ] Request/response schemas do not leak secrets or key material. Key Management - [ ] Key source selectable (env, file, KMS). - [ ] Rotation procedure documented and automated. - [ ] Key usage is logged (audit trail). - [ ] Decryption fails cleanly on key mismatch. Telemetry and Auditing - [ ] Structured logs include org_id + request_id + endpoint. - [ ] Audit log records embed/sign/verify actions. - [ ] Retention + export policies documented. Rate Limits and Abuse Controls - [ ] Per-org throughput limits (embed/verify/sign). - [ ] Burst control and backpressure configured. - [ ] Invalid token attempts rate-limited. Client UX Protections - [ ] Verified badge shown only on server-verified status. - [ ] “Partial” status when attachments fail verification. - [ ] No local-only verification claims. Gateway Protections - [ ] Relay→inbound chain enforced (stamp body for Gmail). - [ ] Attachment header stamping enabled for outbound. - [ ] SMTP STARTTLS behavior correct for local hop. Deployment Hardening - [ ] Service env vars sourced securely (not hardcoded). - [ ] Health endpoints available for monitoring. - [ ] CI verifies enforcement paths (license + scopes).
